newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open higher as no rate hike seen.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open higher as no rate hike seen.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries opened higher Monday morning, continuing to recover from Friday morning's beating, as the weekend gave the market time to rethink where interest rates are headed.
The 30-year bond was at 100-10/32, up 14/32 from late Friday. Its yield fell to 6.48 percent from 6.51 percent.
"The market will be fine; people still need to buy, and (Friday's selloff) gave people an opportunity to buy," said Nelson Thomson, head trader at Yamaichi International (America) Inc.

Most of the market's bounce took place during the Tokyo session, as Japanese trust banks were said to be big buyers of Treasuries. Interest rate swap related buying in five- and 10-year notes also boosted Treasuries overnight, players said.

Traders conceded that the market overreacted Friday to Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's remarks Thursday night suggesting that stock prices might be too high. He also noted that while U.S. inflation appears tame for now, its "future course remains uncertain."
His comments led to a worldwide selloff in stocks and bonds, including Treasuries.

Treasuries had fallen 1 1/2 points early Friday morning as the market interpreted the remarks as Greenspan preparing the market for a rate hike in the future. But, traders said, Greenspan won't raise rates when markets are rallying because it could trigger a crash.
A weaker than expected employment report for November brought Treasuries off early lows and closed little changed Friday, before bouncing Monday morning.
One trader at a large U.S. bank said the market is now viewing Friday as if it never happened. He said the market now looks ahead to inflation and retail sales data later this week.

"The market's going to square positions for those numbers, and get back to its game plan of buying on dips," the trader said. "Friday was a gift and now we can buy (Treasuries) back again (at cheaper levels)."
Market activity this session is expected to be light, with no economic news scheduled for release.
"Today should be a day of rest," Thomson said, adding that he sees the bond trading "plus or minus 10 ticks" from New York opening levels.

Thomson said the market should trade more cautiously for the time being. "It got a dose of reality," he said, referring to the 35-basis-point backup last week. "We learned that, yes, the market can selloff and we could lose money fast.
"I don't think we'll be rushing back to 6 3/8 percent on the long bond anytime soon," he added.
